newsitem.title: CANADA: BioChem Pharma fights Emory patent suit.
newsitem.headline: BioChem Pharma fights Emory patent suit.

text.p: BioChem Pharma Inc said on Tuesday that it filed a response to a patent infringement suit brought by Emory University regarding the company's Epivir/3TC (lamivudine) drug for the treatment of HIV infection and AIDS.
In a statement, BioChem Pharma said the Emory patent claims were invalid.
"The federal courts provide us with the appropriate forum to finally put to rest Emory University's baseless claims to 3TC," said BioChem chief executive Francesco Bellini in a statement.

BioChem Pharma said it responded in court papers filed Tuesday to Emory's allegations. Emory has based its claims to 3TC on its July 1996 U.S. patent, but BioChem Pharma has had the pioneering patent covering 3TC since 1991 and its licensee, Glaxo Wellcome Plc since 1995, the company said.

"The Emory patent is invalid as it fails to comply with the msot fundamental requirements of U.S. patent law. Emory improperly incorporated 3TC into their patent application long after it had been invented and made public by BioChem Pharm and Glaxo Wellcome," the company said.

Atlanta-based Emory had filed a patent infringement suit against BioChem Pharma in July, seeking damages for the sale and distribution of 3TC, an AIDS drug that is marketed under the brand name Epivir in the United States.
Emory was granted a U.S. patent on Epivir in July. Emory's claim rests on the fact that 3TC is one of two mirror image components, called isomers, of a compound called BCH-189.

In its suit, Emory says that BioChem's patent covers how to obtain BCH-189, but not the individual isomer being marketed as 3TC. Emory's patent was granted for a process that separates the isomers that make up BCH-189 and so obtain 3TC.
